title: Every Popular Calisthenics Skill Explained in 10 Minutes
fullText: Push-up. Push-up is the first exercise every human on Earth has done. Usually by accident. Usually face first off a couch as a baby. It's that simple. Plank your body. Lower your chest to the floor. Push back up. Done. That's the whole move. You don't need a tutorial for this, bro. You need to stop being lazy and to actually touch your chest to the ground. And yet, everyone's seen that one guy. Neck poking forward like a chicken, hips drooping, dropping 4 in before he bounces back up, thinking he's knocking out push-ups like Bruce Wayne. [bell] That's not a push-up. That's half a rep and a whole lot of [ __ ] He thinks he's too good for this exercise now. Bro, you never even did one, right? Just don't be the dumbass who does half reps with his ass up in the air. Hands flat on the floor, body dead straight from your head to your heels. Lower yourself until your chest nearly kisses the ground, then push the floor away. That's the whole thing. No deeper meaning, no secret sauce, no tutorial needed. The push-ups got more forms than fingers on one hand. Hands tucked tight in a triangle under your chest. We call it the diamond and it lights your triceps on fire. Hands out wide, chest takes over, feet up on a bench, upper chest eats. Then [ __ ] gets real. Pile your whole weight onto one arm and you've got the archer. And then there's those psychos clapping midair between every rep. Basically training explosive power and looking cool doing it. And the boss of them all. Push your shoulders way out past your hands till your wrists file a complaint. And just like that, you're doing baby plch. Now that's a whole another level. Back in 2022, I couldn't get to a gym. And that was right when those Ziz edits were blowing up everywhere. So, with no gym to go to, I started doing push-ups in my room. And I was weak. No shame in it. I could barely grind out four or five before my arms gave up. But I kept going. And within a couple weeks, the numbers started climbing fast. Then, I wanted more. So, I stuffed a backpack with books, threw it on, and worked with that instead. I'm pretty sure everybody started this exact way, alone in their room, banging out reps on the floor. Anyway, pull up. You hang from a bar, drag your whole body weight up till your chin clears it, then lower down slow. With most exercises, you pick the weight. Here, gravity picks it for you, and it picks your exact body weight every time. That's exactly why the pull-up exposes people. It's the fastest way to find out if a guy is actually strong or just big. Every gym has that one dude repping 120 on bench who can't pull himself up a single time. The bar doesn't lie. Now, the grip changes everything. Palms facing away is the classic pull-up, all back in lats. Flip your palms toward you, and it turns into a chin-up. It's like this, if you don't know. Go wide, and the lats do the heavy lifting. Once your body weight stops being a challenge, you strap a plate to your waist and pile on real weight like this. You think you're just training your back. You're not. A pull-up lights up your lats, your biceps, your forearms, your grip, even your core fighting to stop you from swinging like a wrecking ball. One bar, half your body working at once. And if you can't pull a single one yet, relax. Everybody starts at zero. Just hang there. Dead hangs alone. Build your grip and decompress your spine after a whole day sitting hunched like a shrimp. Then start doing slow negatives. Jump up and lower yourself down like a melting candle. And in a few weeks, that first clean rep is yours. Honestly, I'd stopped training pull-ups for a while, so my numbers dropped hard, and I was basically just dead hanging to get the feel back. And then last week, I'm hanging off the bar at home, and the thing slips out of nowhere. Boom, flat on my ass. Just a little reminder, tighten your bar before you trust it with your body weight, especially if you do pull-ups at home like me. Dip. Long before barbells existed, apes and early humans had been pushing themselves up onto rocks, ledges, and out of trees for millions of years. Every time you plant your hands on something and shove your body weight up off it, that's the same ancient motion your chest, shoulders, and triceps were built for. The dip is just the cleanest version of it. Your torso angle is basically a volume knob, deciding which muscle gets fried. Want a chest dip? Tilt forward, flare your elbows out, tuck your knees back to lock that lean in, and sink down till your chest feels a real stretch. Want a triceps dip? Flip it. Stay upright like a flag pole. Elbows tight to your sides, narrower grip. Let the elbow bend do all the work. Like this guy right here. Can't bang out one yet? Forget everything and just get on the actual parallel bars. Start with negatives. Jump to the top and lower yourself slow as hell, three to five seconds. Then wrap a band under your feet. It helps you most at the bottom where dips are hardest. Few weeks of that and your first clean rep shows up. Once 12 to 15 clean reps feel easy, your body weight stops doing anything for you. Strap a dipping belt around your waist and start hanging plates off it. 20 kilos dangling between your legs and your upper body finally starts growing. That's the beauty of the dip. You don't need some fancy machine or a gym membership. Two parallel bars at the park. Just find something and start pushing. Body weight against gravity. That's it. That's the whole sport. Just don't sacrifice form for ego. Shoulders packed, depth honest, load controlled. Do it right. And the next time you're knocking out reps at the park, the girls walking by won't be able to take their eyes off you, bro. Muscle up. This is where calisthenics stops being exercise and turns into a skill. You hang under the bar, explode up, and instead of stopping at the top like a pull-up, you keep climbing. Roll your chest over the bar and press out until your arms lock above it. Ever hold yourself out of a pool with no ladder? Chest to the edge, flip your hands, push down to stand up. Same motion. The bar is just a pool edge floating over your head. Mechanically, it's a pull-up and a dip stitch together by the nastiest middleman in the gym. That half second where your wrists roll from under the bar to on top of it. Floating, neither pulling nor pressing, is where most attempts die. And the reason is dumb. People pull the bar to their chin. You pull it to your lower chest, almost your belly button because only that height gives your shoulders room to whip forward and roll over the top. On a fixed bar, it's standard. Move to the rings and it turns evil. The ring swing and you need a false grip, wrist already sitting on top before you even pull. Then you have the absolute maniac strapping heavy weights on a dip belt just to do a strict muscle up. That that's a handstand. Right now, your skeleton is balancing your whole body weight upright, bone stacked on bone, and you're pulling it off half asleep and scrolling zero brain cells on the job. Incredible. Flip the same thing onto your hands and your body files for bankruptcy. Wait, we can do this? Nobody told the arms they got drafted into the spine's job and they're pissed about it. It's the handstand, not a strength flex. A hostile takeover where your hands learn from zero. The free ride your legs have coasted on since birth. The shape is insultingly basic. Hands down, body one straight line, toes at the ceiling. Done. Describing it takes 4 seconds. Holding it takes four months of your soul leaving your body. You kick up, hover for two glorious seconds, and topple like a shelf that gave up on the wall. Welcome to the floor. You'll see a lot of it. So, how do you stay up? Not the shoulders, not muscle, not by grunting louder, champ. You balance through your wrists and fingers. Stand on one leg, hand that exact job to your hands. Tip forward, you claw the ground and drag yourself back. Sail past vertical. You ease off and let your heels float in. It never stops. Brace tight, tuck the hips, lock into one rigid plank. That is the hollow body. Go soft and you're just a wet noodle trying to stand up. human flag. Every other calisthenics move keeps you tucked under the bar or stacked on top of it. This one says, "Screw gravity completely." You grab a vertical pole, press yourself sideways off it, and float there, dead horizontal, your whole body sticking straight out into the air like a flag in the wind. People stop walking. Phones come out. It doesn't even look real. Top hand grabs high and pulls down like a lat pull down. Bottom hand grabs low and presses up like an overhead press. Your body one stiff plank locked between the two. Both arms screaming in opposite directions at once. And here's what kills people. They think this is an ab move. Smash six months of ab work, walk up shredded, drop like a sack of bricks. Sure, your obliques fight to keep your hips from sagging, but the engine is your back and shoulders. No lats, no flag. That's why the lean lanky guy floats and the gym bro with the eight pack face plants. Can't hold one yet? Nobody can at first. Dead hangs and pull rows to wake the lats up. Then tuck flag. Knees into your chest so the lever is short enough for your arms to survive. Then straddle, legs split wide. Then the full thing. Body straight as a board. That last one humbles everybody. Oh, and the pull is thick. Way thicker than a bar. Your grip taps out long before your strength does if you sleep on it. World record is over a minute. One man sideways in the air for a full minute. Insane. Front lever. Pull-ups, dips, muscle-ups. They all let you bend your arms and use your biceps to muscle through the front lever throws that out. You hang from a bar, lock your arms dead straight, and pull your whole body up until you're floating face up and horizontal, parallel to the ground. Elbows stay locked the entire time. That straight arm rule changes which muscles run the show. With a bent arm, your biceps take over, lock the elbow, and the job falls to your lats and tears major. The muscles that drag a straight arm down toward your body. The part almost everyone misses is the shoulder blades. You pull them down and back and pin them there the whole hold. Lose that and you collapse instantly. Meanwhile, your abs, glutes, and lower back fight as one unit to stop the bar from folding you in half. Can't hold one? Normal. This is the first real straight arm wall everyone hits. Tuck lever first. Knees to your chest so the lever stays short. Then advance tuck. Hips opening up. Then one leg out. Then straddle. Then full body flat as a board. Every step is a real jump, so do not rush them. The brutal truth. Being jacked barely helps. It's leverage and tendon strength, not size. A lighter guy who trains it holds a clean lever while a huge bench presser sags and drops. Plaunch. And finally, the final boss. The move that eats years of your life and humbles the impatient. There's always that one confident genius certain he'll crack it in 3 months. He's now icing his elbows and googling tendon surgeons. Respect the plunch or it ends. You picture a push-up. Now your feet lift off and your body floats horizontal, parallel to the ground, balanced on nothing but two flat hands. No feet, no support, just pure defiance of common sense. Looks like a glitch in reality. You push your shoulders out past your hands until your body weight stacks over your palms instead of your feet, turning your hands into the fulcrum. The road is long. The plunch lean teaches the position. The tuck balls you up small. The advanced tuck and straddle stretch the lever longer. and the full plunchch almost nobody reaches clean. What wrecks people is forcing that lean before the joints are ready. Muscle gets strong in months, but tendons crawl far slower. And that gap is where injuries breed. Rush it and you don't earn a plunchch, you earn a year of elbow pain. And the best part, your seratus fires overtime here. The same muscle working at the top of a push-up cranked to a deranged extreme. The hardest move on the ladder is really the first move. I'm curious how many push-ups you can do. It would be helpful if you also included your weight. Any guy can load a barbell long enough to get strong, but learning to actually control your own body turns you into a different kind of animal.
